title: The Counter That Lies (Stale Closure)
brief: A counter component increments once from 0 to 1 and then freezes. Fix the stale closure bug.
symptoms: Counter increments to 1 upon mount, then stops counting
Interval callback captures initial count state variable in stale scope closure
Console shows no runtime error

hints.title: Analyze closure state capture
hints.content: The useEffect hook executes once on mount. The setInterval callback closes over the value of count at that moment (0).

hints.title: Functional State Updates
hints.content: Using setCount(prev => prev + 1) guarantees access to the current state without adding count to the dependency array.

explanation: In React, functions created inside components capture state values from the render in which they were created. When an effect creates an interval with an empty dependency array, the interval callback always sees `count` as 0. Using functional state updates (`setCount(prev => prev + 1)`) passes the current state directly to the state updater, avoiding stale closures entirely.

testCases.name: State Updater Functionality
testCases.description: Verifies that state setter uses a functional callback rather than direct count variable reference.

testCases.name: Continuous Tick Execution
testCases.description: Verifies counter increments beyond 1 after multiple interval ticks.

title: The Jumping Hero Banner (CLS)
brief: Dynamic hero banner images load asynchronously and push lower layout elements down abruptly, causing a bad CLS score.
symptoms: Page layout shifts abruptly when image finishes downloading
Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) score exceeds recommended 0.1 threshold
Buttons move unexpectedly under user mouse cursor

hints.title: Reserve dimensional aspect ratio
hints.content: Browsers require explicit dimension ratios or placeholders to calculate box sizes before media assets finish loading.

hints.title: CSS aspect-ratio property
hints.content: Adding aspect-ratio: 16/9 with background fallback holds the exact layout space.

explanation: When an tag lacks explicit dimensions or an aspect-ratio container, the browser defaults its height to 0px until image metadata arrives. Once loaded, the browser reflows the entire page, shifting downstream content downwards. Reserving container dimensions using CSS `aspect-ratio` guarantees zero shift.

testCases.name: Zero Dimension Shift
testCases.description: Checks if container height remains identical before and after image load.

testCases.name: Aspect Ratio Specification
testCases.description: Ensures aspect-ratio or explicit height constraints are declared on the hero container.

title: The Slow Resizing Tab (Retained Event Listener)
brief: A window resize handler is registered inside useEffect without an unmount cleanup function, causing memory leaks.
symptoms: Memory usage steadily climbs every time user navigates to the route
Multiple duplicate window resize handlers trigger simultaneously on resize
Unmounted component references remain trapped in memory heap

hints.title: Effect Lifecycle Cleanups
hints.content: Return a function from useEffect to detach global window or document event listeners.

hints.title: Reference equality for handlers
hints.content: Ensure the handleResize function reference passed to removeEventListener matches the exact one attached during addEventListener.

explanation: Global objects like `window` outlive React component lifecycles. Adding an event listener to `window` inside `useEffect` creates a persistent reference to the component instance. Without removing the listener upon component unmount, garbage collection is prevented and listeners accumulate infinitely on subsequent mounts.

testCases.name: EventListener Detachment
testCases.description: Verifies that window.removeEventListener is invoked with matching handler on component unmount.

testCases.name: Heap Garbage Collection
testCases.description: Confirms listener count resets to zero when navigating away.

title: Out-of-Order Search Results (Network Race)
brief: Rapid search input displays stale results from earlier, slower network responses instead of the latest search query.
symptoms: Typing 'React' shows results for 'Rea' because query 'Rea' took longer to respond
Network waterfall shows out-of-order response completions
UI search state mismatches actual input field value

hints.title: AbortController API
hints.content: Create an AbortController inside the effect and abort it in the effect cleanup return function.

hints.title: Ignore AbortError
hints.content: Catch errors in fetch promise chain and filter out expected 'AbortError' exceptions.

explanation: Network responses arrive asynchronously; latency varies per query. If a user types 'a' then 'ab', the request for 'a' may take 500ms while 'ab' takes 100ms. Without cancellation, response 'a' arrives last and overwrites response 'ab'. Using `AbortController` or boolean flags inside `useEffect` discards stale network responses.

testCases.name: Abort Signal Attachment
testCases.description: Verifies AbortController signal is passed into fetch request options.

testCases.name: Inflight Abort Execution
testCases.description: Verifies controller.abort() is called when query changes prior to completion.

title: Unlabeled Icon Buttons & Focus Leak (Accessibility)
brief: Icon-only buttons lack accessible names for screen readers, and custom popovers fail keyboard focus control.
symptoms: Screen readers announce 'button' with no descriptive text
Keyboard Tab navigation bypasses active drawer controls
Fails WCAG 2.1 Name, Role, Value (4.1.2) compliance
brokenCode:
/* ❌ Icon-only button with no screen reader label or aria-label */
<button className="p-2 rounded-md hover:bg-accent">
  <TrashIcon className="h-4 w-4" />
</button>
fixedCode: /* ✅ Accessible button with aria-label and visually hidden fallback text */

hints.title: Provide accessible labels
hints.content: Use aria-label or sr-only span elements to give icon buttons an accessible text name.

hints.title: Hide decorative SVG icons
hints.content: Mark SVG icons with aria-hidden='true' so screen readers don't read raw SVG path vectors.

explanation: Screen reader users rely on accessible names generated from element text content, `aria-label`, or `aria-labelledby`. An icon-only `<button>` containing solely an `<svg>` tag has no text, causing screen readers to output uninformative names like 'button' or 'unlabeled'.

testCases.name: Accessible Name Check
testCases.description: Verifies button element contains aria-label or .sr-only accessible text string.

testCases.name: Decorative Icon Suppression
testCases.description: Verifies embedded SVG icons carry aria-hidden='true'.

title: The Laggy Product Data Grid (Unmemoized Callbacks)
brief: Passing new object literals and unmemoized callbacks into list items causes 500+ child components to re-render on every keystroke.
symptoms: Typing in filter search box produces noticeable keystroke latency (>100ms)
React DevTools Profiler shows all 500 list items re-rendering on every key press
CPU profiling indicates excessive reconciliation overhead

hints.title: Reference equality in props
hints.content: Inline function expressions () => ... create a brand new function reference on every render, invalidating child memoization.

hints.title: useCallback & useMemo
hints.content: Wrap event handlers in useCallback and derived filter calculations in useMemo.

explanation: Components wrapped in `React.memo` skip rendering only if all props retain shallow equality (`===`). Passing inline object literals (`style={{...}}`) or inline callbacks (`() => ...`) creates fresh references on every parent render, forcing every child component to re-render unnecessarily.

testCases.name: Callback Reference Stability
testCases.description: Confirms handler callback reference remains stable across filter state updates.

testCases.name: Re-render Threshold Optimization
testCases.description: Verifies child component render count drops from 500+ to zero for unaffected rows.

title: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'map')
brief: Accessing array methods on asynchronous state before initial fetch completes triggers a blank screen runtime crash.
symptoms: White screen crash on initial page load before API resolves
Uncaught TypeError: Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'map')
App breaks unless state is initialized or guarded with optional chaining

hints.title: Default state initialization
hints.content: Initialize array state with useState([]) or default parameter values.

hints.title: Optional chaining & Nullish fallback
hints.content: Use (data ?? []).map(...) or data?.map(...) to safely evaluate potentially undefined data.

explanation: React components render synchronously prior to asynchronous `useEffect` execution. When `useState()` is initialized without parameters, `data` is `undefined` on the first render pass. Calling `.map()` on `undefined` causes JavaScript to throw an uncaught `TypeError` and unmount the component tree.

testCases.name: Initial Render Guard
testCases.description: Verifies component renders gracefully without error during initial loading phase.

testCases.name: Safe Collection Iteration
testCases.description: Confirms array mapping succeeds safely when data arrives or is empty.

title: Broken React App: The Uncapped Re-render Storm
brief: Updating state directly inside an un-guarded useEffect dependency array creates an infinite render cycle that freezes the browser.
symptoms: Browser tab freezes or crashes with 'Too many re-renders. React limits the number of renders'
CPU usage spikes to 100%
Network request spam or exponential state updates

hints.title: Dependency array mutation loop
hints.content: Updating a state variable inside useEffect while including that same variable in the dependency array causes an endless loop.

hints.title: Functional updater & empty deps
hints.content: Use functional state updates setSettings(prev => ...) and remove the state object from the effect dependencies.

explanation: Every time `setSettings` executes, React creates a new object reference. Because `settings` is listed in `useEffect`'s dependency array, React detects a change (`oldObject !== newObject`) and re-runs the effect immediately, triggering `setSettings` again in an infinite loop.

testCases.name: Bounded Render Cycle
testCases.description: Verifies component render count remains stable and does not exceed maximum update depth.

testCases.name: Dependency Array Optimization
testCases.description: Ensures state setters inside effects do not depend on mutated object references.

title: The Cart Total That Isn't a Number (Unsafe Type Assertion)
brief: A cart total renders as 'NaN' in production even though TypeScript reports no errors. Find where an unsafe type assertion let bad data through.
symptoms: TypeScript compiles with zero errors
Cart total displays 'NaN' whenever a product's price field is missing from the API response
No runtime error is thrown -- the page just shows wrong data

hints.title: What does 'as Product[]' actually check?
hints.content: Nothing at runtime -- 'as' is a compile-time-only promise to the type checker. If the real API response doesn't match, TypeScript won't catch it.

hints.title: Type unknown, then narrow
hints.content: Typing the parsed response as unknown and writing a real runtime check (a type guard) catches the mismatch instead of silently trusting it.

explanation: A type assertion (as Product[]) tells TypeScript to trust your model without verifying it -- it performs no runtime check. When the API sends an item missing a price field, the assertion still succeeds at compile time, and the missing value quietly becomes undefined, turning the sum into NaN with no error anywhere. Typing the response as unknown and validating it with a real type guard (or a schema validator) closes this gap.

testCases.name: Handles missing price field
testCases.description: Verifies the function doesn't silently produce NaN when an item is missing its price.

testCases.name: Correct total for valid data
testCases.description: Verifies the total is still computed correctly for a normal, well-formed response.

title: The Comment That Ran a Script (Stored XSS)
brief: A comment section renders user-submitted HTML directly. Find and fix the stored XSS vulnerability without breaking legitimate rich-text comments.
symptoms: A comment containing a <script> tag executes when any user views the page
The vulnerability persists for every viewer, not just the person who posted it
No error appears in the console -- the injected script simply runs

hints.title: Where does React's default safety break?
hints.content: Plain JSX interpolation like {text} escapes content automatically. dangerouslySetInnerHTML explicitly opts out of that protection.

hints.title: Don't hand-roll sanitization
hints.content: Use a maintained library like DOMPurify rather than writing your own escaping logic -- XSS payload variations are easy to miss by hand.

explanation: This is stored XSS: the malicious payload is saved with the comment and executes for every subsequent viewer, since dangerouslySetInnerHTML renders the raw string as real HTML rather than escaping it. Since this component has a genuine need to render rich text, the fix isn't to remove dangerouslySetInnerHTML -- it's to run the content through a sanitization library like DOMPurify first, stripping executable content while preserving legitimate formatting.

testCases.name: Strips script tags
testCases.description: Verifies a comment containing a <script> tag no longer executes after sanitization.

testCases.name: Preserves legitimate formatting
testCases.description: Verifies safe tags like <b> and <em> still render correctly after sanitization.

title: The Test That Tests Nothing (Over-Mocked Validation)
brief: A signup form's test suite is green, but a real validation bug still shipped to production. Find why the test can't actually catch it.
symptoms: The test suite passes with 100% green checks
A user reported that invalid emails are being accepted in production
The relevant test claims to cover 'invalid email rejection'

hints.title: What is validateEmail's mock actually doing?
hints.content: The mock always returns true, meaning the exact validation logic the test claims to verify never actually runs during the test.

hints.title: Mock the boundary, not the logic under test
hints.content: Only mock genuine external boundaries (network, timers). Mocking the function you're trying to verify defeats the test's purpose.

explanation: This test mocked validateEmail directly, replacing the real logic with a function that always returns true -- so the test could never have caught the validation bug, no matter how broken the real implementation was. It also never actually asserted anything about the resulting UI. The fix is to let the real validation logic run (remove the mock) and assert on the user-visible outcome: a validation error message appearing for invalid input.

testCases.name: Real validation logic executes
testCases.description: Verifies the test no longer mocks out the function it claims to be testing.

testCases.name: Asserts on visible error
testCases.description: Verifies the test actually checks for a user-visible validation error message.

title: One Bad Widget, One Blank Page (Unscoped Error Boundary)
brief: A single failing third-party widget blanks the entire dashboard, including the navigation. Fix the error boundary scoping without touching the widget itself.
symptoms: When the StockTicker widget throws during render, the whole page goes blank
Navigation and unrelated dashboard sections disappear along with the broken widget
The app has exactly one ErrorBoundary, wrapping the entire tree

hints.title: Where should the boundary actually sit?
hints.content: Move Nav and MainContent outside the boundary entirely, and wrap only the genuinely risky component.

hints.title: One boundary per independent risky section
hints.content: A single app-wide boundary means any failure anywhere blanks the whole page -- barely better than no boundary at all.

explanation: Wrapping the entire app in one error boundary means a crash anywhere -- even in a minor, non-critical widget -- takes down everything, including navigation the user still needs. Scoping the boundary to just the risky, independent section (here, StockTicker) means only that section shows a fallback while the rest of the page, like Nav and MainContent, keeps working normally.

testCases.name: Nav survives a StockTicker crash
testCases.description: Verifies Nav and MainContent still render when StockTicker throws.

testCases.name: Fallback shows only for the broken section
testCases.description: Verifies the fallback message appears in place of StockTicker specifically, not the whole page.

title: The Save That Silently Failed (Swallowed Promise Rejection)
brief: A 'Save' button shows no error, but the data never actually persists. Find why the failure is being swallowed silently.
symptoms: Clicking Save shows no error message and no loading indicator gets stuck
The network tab shows the save request actually failed with a 500
The UI behaves as if the save succeeded

hints.title: Is the fetch actually being waited on?
hints.content: Without await, showSuccessToast() runs immediately, before the request even resolves -- regardless of whether it succeeds or fails.

hints.title: Does fetch reject on a 500 response?
hints.content: fetch only rejects on a network failure, not an HTTP error status -- you have to check res.ok yourself and throw explicitly.

explanation: Two separate bugs compound here: the missing await means showSuccessToast() runs unconditionally, without ever checking the request's outcome; and even with await added, fetch doesn't reject on a 4xx/5xx response, so a failed save with no res.ok check still looks successful. Both the await and the explicit status check are needed to surface the real failure to the user.

testCases.name: Shows an error toast on a failed save
testCases.description: Verifies a 500 response triggers a visible error state instead of a silent success toast.

testCases.name: Shows success only after a real 2xx response
testCases.description: Verifies the success toast only appears once the save has genuinely completed.

title: The Error That Points Nowhere Useful (Minified Stack Trace)
brief: A production error report shows a stack trace pointing to `chunk-7f3a91.js:1:48213` with no useful information. Diagnose why, and fix the build config so future errors are actually debuggable.
symptoms: Production error logs show minified variable names and single-letter function names
The stack trace line/column numbers don't correspond to any readable source location
The same error is easy to reproduce and read locally in dev, but useless from the production log

hints.title: What does minification actually remove?
hints.content: Minification strips readable names and collapses code, which is great for bundle size but makes raw stack traces meaningless without a map back to the original source.

hints.title: What connects a minified line back to real source?
hints.content: A source map file records the mapping from minified output back to original file/line/column -- your error tracking tool needs access to it to de-minify traces.

explanation: Minified production code trades readability for smaller bundle size, and a raw stack trace against minified code just points to compressed, renamed code with no useful information. Enabling sourcemap generation in the build config lets your error tracking tool (uploaded separately, not served publicly) reconstruct the original file, function name, and line number from a minified stack trace -- turning `chunk-7f3a91.js:1:48213` back into `ProfileForm.tsx:42`.

testCases.name: Source maps are generated on build
testCases.description: Verifies the build output includes .map files alongside the minified JS.

testCases.name: A de-minified trace resolves to real source location
testCases.description: Verifies a thrown error's stack trace can be mapped back to the actual source file and line.

title: The Sidebar That Doesn't Know It's Selected (Prop Drilling Gone Stale)
brief: A selected sidebar item stops highlighting correctly after adding a new layer of components. Find where the selection state got disconnected.
symptoms: Clicking a sidebar item calls the onSelect handler (confirmed via console.log)
The visual highlight doesn't move to the newly selected item
A newly added wrapper component sits between the state owner and the item that reads it

hints.title: What does useState(selectedId) actually capture?
hints.content: useState's argument is only used for the *initial* render -- it doesn't re-sync with the prop on every subsequent render.

hints.title: Does this wrapper need local state at all?
hints.content: If a component is just forwarding a value it received as a prop, copying it into local state usually isn't needed -- pass the prop straight through.

explanation: SidebarWrapper copied the incoming selectedId prop into local state with useState, but useState's initial value is only used on the very first render -- it doesn't track subsequent prop changes automatically. So every later click updates the real selectedId in the parent, but SidebarWrapper's stale localSelectedId snapshot never updates, and the highlight never moves. Since this component has no actual reason to own local state here, the fix is simply to pass the prop straight through instead of shadowing it.

testCases.name: Highlight moves on selection
testCases.description: Verifies clicking a different sidebar item visually updates which item is highlighted.

testCases.name: Selection persists through the wrapper across re-renders
testCases.description: Verifies selectedId stays in sync with the parent even after unrelated re-renders.

title: The Style That Won't Apply (Specificity War)
brief: A utility class meant to override a component's text color has no visible effect. Find which rule is actually winning the cascade, and fix it without reaching for !important.
symptoms: Adding class="text-danger" to a button doesn't change its text color
The .text-danger rule is confirmed present in the stylesheet with the expected color value
DevTools shows the rule as present but struck through (overridden)

hints.title: Count the selectors in each competing rule
hints.content: .card .btn.btn-primary has three class selectors chained; .text-danger has only one. Specificity is compared by count, not by source order alone.

hints.title: Does load order matter here?
hints.content: Load order only breaks ties between selectors of EQUAL specificity -- it never overrides a higher-specificity selector, no matter which stylesheet loads last.

explanation: CSS specificity is compared before source order ever comes into play. `.card .btn.btn-primary` has three class selectors combined, giving it higher specificity than the single-class `.text-danger`, so it wins regardless of which stylesheet loads later. Reaching for !important would technically fix this instance but creates a worse long-term problem -- it becomes the next thing someone has to fight. The more durable fix is either matching specificity deliberately or keeping component styles from accumulating deeply-nested, multi-class selectors that make simple overrides hard.

testCases.name: text-danger applies over the component's own color
testCases.description: Verifies the danger text color visually wins without using !important.

testCases.name: No !important was introduced
testCases.description: Verifies the fix addresses specificity structurally rather than forcing an override.
